Cadillac Williams :: Professional career :: Tampa Bay Buccaneers :: Injuries :: chunk_0005
In October 2007, Williams suffered a torn [patellar tendon](/wiki/Patellar_tendon "Patellar tendon") to his right knee against Carolina, which required surgery and ended his season. Doctors were doubtful he would come back to full strength after this devastating injury. Williams, however, said that he had "no doubt" that he would play in 2008.

In mid-season of 2008, Williams began practicing with the team and was listed as questionable on the official injury report. In November, he was taken off the [Physically Unable to Perform](/wiki/Physically_Unable_to_Perform "Physically Unable to Perform") list and added to the active roster. He played in his first game in 14 months against Detroit. On November 30 against the Saints, he scored his first touchdown since his return. One month later, however, during the final game of the season on December 28, Williams suffered another torn patellar tendon, this time in his left knee.

The second tear was not as severe as the first, but Williams again endured surgery and an intense period of rehab to get back on the field. He returned to game action during the 2009 preseason and was the Bucs' starting running back to open the regular season, becoming the first NFL player to return from patellar tendon tears in both knees.[[19]](#cite_note-19) On December 27, Williams had his first 100-yard rushing game in two seasons for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and finished with 823 yards, the second highest total of his NFL career.. Williams was narrowly edged for the AP 2009 [Comeback Player of the Year Award](/wiki/National_Football_League_Comeback_Player_of_the_Year_Award "National Football League Comeback Player of the Year Award") by [Tom Brady](/wiki/Tom_Brady "Tom Brady"), finishing second with 15 votes. He rushed for 821 yards on 210 carries with a 3.9 average and four touchdowns. He also caught 29 passes for 219 yards and 3 touchdowns.

Saudi Arabia :: Etymology :: chunk_0005
See also: [House of Saud](/wiki/House_of_Saud "House of Saud") and [Arab (etymology)](/wiki/Arab_(etymology) "Arab (etymology)")

Following the amalgamation of the [Kingdom of Hejaz](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hejaz "Kingdom of Hejaz") and [Nejd](/wiki/Sultanate_of_Nejd "Sultanate of Nejd"), [Abdulaziz](/wiki/Ibn_Saud "Ibn Saud") issued a royal decree on 23 September 1932 naming the new state *al-Mamlaka al-ʿArabiyya as-Suʿūdiyya* ([Arabic](/wiki/Arabic "Arabic") المملكة العربية السعودية), which is normally translated as "the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia" in English,[[41]](#cite_note-US_State_Dept_Saudi_Arabia-46) but literally means "the **Saudi Arab Kingdom**",[[42]](#cite_note-47) or "the **Saudi Kingdom of Arabia**" (compare [the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan](/wiki/The_Hashemite_Kingdom_of_Jordan "The Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan")).

The word "Saudi" is derived from the element *as-Suʿūdīyya* in the Arabic name of the country, which is a type of adjective known as a *[nisba](/wiki/Nisba_(onomastics) "Nisba (onomastics)"),* formed from the dynastic name of the Saudi royal family, the [Al Saud](/wiki/House_of_Saud "House of Saud") ([Arabic](/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): آل سعود). Its inclusion expresses the view that the country is the personal possession of the royal family.[[43]](#cite_note-48)[[44]](#cite_note-Kamrava-49) *Al Saud* is an [Arabic name](/wiki/Arabic_name "Arabic name") formed by adding the word *Al*, meaning "family of" or "House of",[[45]](#cite_note-50) to the personal name of an ancestor. In the case of Al Saud, this is [Saud ibn Muhammad ibn Muqrin](/wiki/Saud_ibn_Muhammad_ibn_Muqrin "Saud ibn Muhammad ibn Muqrin"), the father of the dynasty's 18th-century founder, [Muhammad bin Saud](/wiki/Muhammad_bin_Saud "Muhammad bin Saud").[[46]](#cite_note-51)

Main article: [History of Saudi Arabia](/wiki/History_of_Saudi_Arabia "History of Saudi Arabia")

Main article: [Harvard Law School](/wiki/Harvard_Law_School "Harvard Law School")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/47/Langdell.jpg)](/wiki/File:Langdell.jpg)

[Christopher Columbus Langdell](/wiki/Christopher_Columbus_Langdell "Christopher Columbus Langdell"), an influential dean of [Harvard Law School](/wiki/Harvard_Law_School "Harvard Law School") from 1875 to 1890

The establishment of Harvard Law School in 1817 was made possible by a 1779 bequest from [Isaac Royall Jr.](/wiki/Isaac_Royall_Jr. "Isaac Royall Jr."); it is the oldest continuously operating law school in the nation.[[129]](#cite_note-Gershman-130) It was a small operation and grew slowly. By 1827, it was down to one faculty member. [Nathan Dane](/wiki/Nathan_Dane "Nathan Dane"), a prominent alumnus, endowed the Dane Professorship of Law and insisted that it be given to then Supreme Court Justice [Joseph Story](/wiki/Joseph_Story "Joseph Story"). For a while, the school was called Dane Law School.[[130]](#cite_note-131) Story's belief in the need for an elite law school based on merit and dedicated to public service helped build the school's reputation at the time. Enrollment remained low as academic legal education was considered to be of little added benefit to apprenticeships in legal practice.

Radical reform came in the 1870s, under Dean [Christopher Columbus Langdell](/wiki/Christopher_Columbus_Langdell "Christopher Columbus Langdell") (1826–1906).[[131]](#cite_note-132) Its new curriculum set the national standard and was copied widely in the United States. Langdell developed the [case method](/wiki/Casebook_method "Casebook method") of teaching law, based on his belief that law could be studied as a "science" gave university legal education a reason for being distinct from vocational preparation. The school introduced a first-year curriculum that was widely imitated, based on classes in [contracts](/wiki/Contracts "Contracts"), [property](/wiki/Property "Property"), [torts](/wiki/Torts "Torts"), [criminal law](/wiki/Criminal_law "Criminal law") and [civil procedure](/wiki/Civil_procedure "Civil procedure").

There are two living retired justices of the Supreme Court of the United States: Anthony Kennedy and Stephen Breyer. As retired justices, they no longer participate in the work of the Supreme Court, but may be designated for temporary assignments to sit on lower federal courts, usually the [United States Courts of Appeals](/wiki/United_States_Courts_of_Appeals "United States Courts of Appeals"). Such assignments are formally made by the chief justice, on request of the [chief judge](/wiki/Chief_judge_(United_States) "Chief judge (United States)") of the lower court and with the consent of the retired justice. The status of a retired justice is analogous to that of a circuit or district court judge who has taken [senior status](/wiki/Senior_status "Senior status"), and eligibility of a Supreme Court justice to assume retired status (rather than simply resign from the bench) is governed by the same age and service criteria.

In recent times, justices tend to strategically plan their decisions to leave the bench with personal, institutional, ideological, partisan, and political factors playing a role.[[168]](#cite_note-168)[[169]](#cite_note-169) The fear of mental decline and death often motivates justices to step down. The desire to maximize the court's strength and legitimacy through one retirement at a time, when the court is in recess and during non-presidential election years suggests a concern for institutional health. Finally, especially in recent decades, many justices have timed their departure to coincide with a philosophically compatible president holding office, to ensure that a like-minded successor would be appointed.[[170]](#cite_note-170)[[171]](#cite_note-171)

**Franklin Delano Roosevelt**[[a]](#cite_note-2) (January 30, 1882 – April 12, 1945), also known by his initials **FDR**, was the 32nd [president of the United States](/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States"), serving from 1933 until his death in 1945. He is the [longest-serving US president](/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_time_in_office "List of presidents of the United States by time in office") and the only one to have served more than two terms. His [first two terms](/wiki/Presidency_of_Franklin_D._Roosevelt_(1933%E2%80%931941) "Presidency of Franklin D. Roosevelt (1933–1941)") were centered on combating the [Great Depression](/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression"), while his [third and fourth](/wiki/Presidency_of_Franklin_D._Roosevelt_(1941%E2%80%931945) "Presidency of Franklin D. Roosevelt (1941–1945)") focused on US involvement in [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). A member of the [Democratic Party](/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"), Roosevelt served in the [New York State Senate](/wiki/New_York_State_Senate "New York State Senate") from 1911 to 1913 and as the 44th [governor of New York](/wiki/Governor_of_New_York "Governor of New York") from 1929 to 1932.

Singapore is one of the world's wealthiest countries *per capita*, but its [Gini coefficient](/wiki/Gini_coefficient "Gini coefficient") is high in comparison to developed countries. Statistics on income inequality are published by the Singapore Department of Statistics.[[175]](#cite_note-178) Without taking taxes and social transfers into account, Singapore's [gini coefficient](/wiki/Gini_coefficient "Gini coefficient") puts the country in the medium range. Nevertheless, the country remains on the "very high" category on the inequality-adjusted human development index (IHDI), a ranking similar to the [Human Development Index](/wiki/Human_Development_Index "Human Development Index") (HDI), but with [inequality](/wiki/Economic_inequality "Economic inequality") also accounted for.[[176]](#cite_note-IHDI-179)

The name *Hippeastrum* was first given to the genus by [Herbert](/wiki/William_Herbert_(botanist) "William Herbert (botanist)"),[[30]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerbert1821-31) being derived from the [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek "Ancient Greek"),[[31]](#cite_note-Math99-32) meaning a "knight's star" from *ἱππεύς* ([hippeus](/wiki/Hippeus "Hippeus"), mounted [knight](/wiki/Knight "Knight")) and *ἄστρον* ([astron](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E1%BC%84%CF%83%CF%84%CF%81%CE%BF%CE%BD#Ancient_Greek "wikt:ἄστρον"), star), to describe the first recognized species, *Hippeastrum reginae*. Herbert proposed to call the genus, which he distinguished from Linnaeus' *Amaryllis*, *Hippeastrum*, or "knight's-star-lily". He states;

> "I have named [them] *Hippeastrum* or Knights-star-lily, pursuing the idea which gave rise to the name Equestris" (p.12).[[30]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerbert1821-31)

Herbert's fourteen species included this *Hippeastrum equestre*.[[31]](#cite_note-Math99-32) This '[equine](/wiki/Equine "Equine")' connection refers to [Carl Linnaeus the Younger](/wiki/Carl_Linnaeus_the_Younger "Carl Linnaeus the Younger") who had named (in an unpublished manuscript) a [West Indian](/wiki/West_Indies "West Indies") species as *Amaryllis equestris*, because of its similarity to the African genus *[Amaryllis](/wiki/Amaryllis "Amaryllis")*. This name and attribution was first published by [William Aiton](/wiki/William_Aiton "William Aiton") in 1789, in his *[Hortus Kewensis](/wiki/Hortus_Kewensis "Hortus Kewensis")*.[[32]](#cite_note-Aiton-33) Which species this was is not known precisely.
